questions.question: What is the difference between widening and narrowing type conversion in Java?
questions.title: Widening vs Narrowing Type Conversion in Java
questions.direct_answer: A widening primitive conversion moves to a type whose set of values is generally broader and usually needs no cast, such as `int` to `long`. It can still lose precision—for example, a large `int` or `long` converted to `float`. A narrowing conversion usually needs an explicit cast and can discard range, precision, or a fractional part.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java's type system and automatic vs manual conversions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that narrowing truncates (doesn't round) — (int) 3.9 gives 3, not 4
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the widening order byte → short → int → long → float → double, and explain why narrowing can lose data

sections.title: Going Up a Type Is Free; Coming Back Down Needs Your Signature
sections.content:
A **widening primitive conversion** is one Java usually allows without an explicit cast, such as `int` to `long` or `float` to `double`. It avoids some range loss, but it is not always exact: a large `int` or `long` may be rounded when converted to `float`, and a `long` may lose exactness as a `double`.

A **narrowing primitive conversion** moves to a type that cannot represent every source value, such as `double` to `int` or `long` to `short`, so an explicit cast is normally required. Integer narrowing can discard high-order bits. Floating-to-integer narrowing removes the fractional part toward zero, then clamps values outside the target range; NaN becomes zero.

The cast grants the conversion—it does not validate business meaning. Check bounds and precision where loss is unacceptable, and use decimal arithmetic with an explicit rounding rule for money.

sections.title: The Type Hierarchy: Widening Goes Up Freely, Narrowing Goes Down With a Cast
sections.content:
Common numeric widening paths include `byte → short → int → long → float → double`, plus `char → int → long → float → double`. A conversion may skip intermediate types.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    B["byte"] --> S["short"] --> I["int"] --> L["long"] --> F["float"] --> D["double"]
    C["char"] --> I
    D -. "explicit narrowing cast" .-> I
    L -. "explicit narrowing cast" .-> S
```

Automatic does not mean exact: `long → float` is widening but can round the value.

sections.title: Widening vs Narrowing at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Widening|~Smaller to larger|int to long to double|implicit, automatic|No range loss in many cases; precision may still be lost
blue|Narrowing|~Larger to smaller|double to int|explicit cast required|may lose data
emerald|Widening order|~byte to double|byte short int long|then float double|each step is safe
rose|Watch out|~Narrowing truncates|(int) 9.9 is 9|overflow wraps silently|byte 300 becomes 44

sections.title: Widening vs Narrowing Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Widening | Narrowing |
|---|---|---|
| Direction | Smaller to larger type | Larger to smaller type |
| Syntax | Implicit, automatic | Explicit cast required |
| Data loss | None — usually implicit | Possible truncation/overflow |
| Example | `int` to `long` | `double` to `int` |
| When | Assignment, method calls | Only with an explicit cast |

sections.title: The Line That Looks Harmless but Won't Compile
sections.content:
The most common first encounter with narrowing is an accident. You compute something as a `double`, then try to store it in an `int` without thinking about the gap between the two types.

```java
double d = 9.99;
int i = d; // COMPILE ERROR: narrowing requires an explicit cast
```

Java stops you here on purpose. It will not silently drop the `.99` for you — it makes you write the cast so the data loss is your decision, not a hidden side effect.

sections.title: Widening Just Works; Narrowing Asks You to Take Responsibility
sections.content:
Once you fix the line, the contrast becomes obvious. Widening assignments need nothing. Narrowing assignments need a cast in front, and that cast is your acknowledgement that something might be lost.

```java
long l = 100;        // widening: int -> long, implicit and safe
double big = l;      // widening: long -> double, implicit
int i = (int) 9.99;  // narrowing: explicit cast, truncates to 9
byte b = (byte) 300; // narrowing overflow: wraps to 44 (no exception)
```

Look closely at the last line — the cast compiles, runs, and gives you `44` with no warning at all. The cast silences the compiler; it does not protect the value. That is exactly why you only narrow when you have checked the value fits.

sections.title: When Each Conversion Happens
sections.content: Use widening when the destination API expects a wider primitive type, while checking whether floating-point exactness matters. Use narrowing only when the target representation is intentional and the input range has been considered. For exact narrowing between integer types, helpers such as `Math.toIntExact(long)` can report overflow instead of silently discarding bits. A direct floating-to-integer cast is appropriate only when truncation and its out-of-range rules are the desired behavior.

sections.title: The Traps That Turn a Cast Into a Silent Bug
sections.content:
- **Calling every widening conversion lossless:** `int` or `long` to `float`, and some `long` to `double`, can lose exactness.
- **Expecting floating-to-integer casting to round:** it truncates toward zero for finite in-range values.
- **Expecting an overflow exception from a primitive cast:** many narrowing conversions return a changed value instead.
- **Calling a cast validation:** it only requests the conversion.
- **Using binary floating point for exact money:** use a decimal representation and explicit rounding policy.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Widening**: usually implicit, such as `int` to `long`.
- **Precision warning**: `int`/`long` to `float`, and `long` to `double`, can lose exactness.
- **Narrowing**: normally needs a cast and may lose range or a fractional part.
- **A cast does not validate the value**; check bounds when loss is unacceptable.
- **Money**: prefer decimal arithmetic such as `BigDecimal`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Widening conversions are the conversions Java usually allows without a cast, such as int to long. Narrowing conversions, such as double to int, normally require an explicit cast because the target cannot represent every source value.

I would avoid saying Widening can still lose floating-point precision. A large int converted to float can be rounded because float has fewer precision bits, and long to double can also lose exactness. A cast only tells the compiler the conversion is intentional; it does not guarantee the result is suitable for the application.

questions.question: How do you convert a String to an int and an int to a String in Java?
questions.title: String to int and int to String Conversion in Java
questions.direct_answer: Convert text to a primitive integer with `Integer.parseInt(text)` and to an `Integer` with `Integer.valueOf(text)`; invalid syntax or an out-of-range value throws `NumberFormatException`. Convert an int to text with `Integer.toString(value)` or `String.valueOf(value)`. These are parsing and formatting operations, not casts.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Java knowledge — type conversion is done in almost every real application
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Integer.parseInt on a non-numeric string without try-catch, or casting a String to int directly (which doesn't work)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish parseInt (returns primitive) vs valueOf (returns Integer object), and mention NumberFormatException handling

sections.title: Why You Can't Cast "42" to a Number — You Have to Parse It
sections.content:
Turning `"42"` into the numeric value 42 is **parsing**, not casting. Primitive numeric casts convert between numeric representations, and reference casts check compatible reference types; neither interprets the characters of a String as a number.

`Integer.parseInt(text)` returns a primitive `int`. `Integer.valueOf(text)` returns an `Integer` after parsing and can reuse wrapper objects according to `Integer.valueOf(int)` rules. Both throw `NumberFormatException` if the text is not valid for the selected radix or the value is outside the int range. They do not accept surrounding whitespace unless the caller removes it deliberately.

For the other direction, `Integer.toString(value)` and `String.valueOf(value)` return decimal text. Radix overloads support bases such as binary or hexadecimal. Define invalid-input behavior at the boundary rather than always catching and inventing a default.

sections.title: String ↔ int Conversion: Two Different Tools for Two Different Directions
sections.content:
The diagram below shows the two conversion paths. Notice that casting is crossed out — it does not work here. Each direction has its own dedicated tool. ```mermaid flowchart LR STR["\"42\"
(String)"] NUM["42
(int)"] OBJ["Integer
(object)"] STR -->|"Integer.parseInt()
→ primitive int"| NUM STR -->|"Integer.valueOf()
→ Integer object"| OBJ OBJ -->|"auto-unboxing"| NUM NUM -->|"String.valueOf()
or Integer.toString()"| STR CAST["(int) str
COMPILE ERROR"] style CAST fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444,color:#991b1b ``` ParseInt is your go-to for String → int. String.valueOf is your go-to for int → String. The red box is the thing freshers try that does not compile.

sections.title: String / int Conversion at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|String to int|~parseInt(str)|returns a primitive int|valueOf returns Integer|the common case
blue|int to String|~String.valueOf(n)|Integer.toString(n)|"" + n (less clear)|preferred: valueOf
emerald|Failure|~NumberFormatException|on "12abc"|wrap untrusted input|trim it first
rose|Radix|~parseInt(s, 16)|hex/binary/octal|bases 2 to 36|toString(n, radix) too

sections.title: The Line Everyone Tries First That Refuses to Compile
sections.content:
The instinct is to treat text-to-number like any other conversion and slap a cast in front of it. Java rejects it before the program ever runs.

```java
String text = "42";
int n = (int) text; // COMPILE ERROR: cannot cast String to int
```

This is not a runtime surprise you can catch — it is a hard compile error, because `String` and `int` share no inheritance relationship for the cast to walk.

sections.title: The Four Calls That Cover Almost Every Real Conversion
When to Use Each Method
sections.content: Use `parseInt` when the required result is a primitive int and `valueOf` when an Integer object is specifically needed. Use radix overloads when the input contract is not decimal. At an external-input boundary, decide whether invalid text should produce a validation result, a mapped exception, or propagation; do not automatically return zero because zero may be a valid value. Trim only if the input format explicitly allows surrounding whitespace.

sections.title: Where String-to-int Conversions Blow Up in Production
sections.content:
- **Trying `(int) "42"`:** parsing text is not a cast.
- **Assuming whitespace is accepted:** `parseInt` does not trim the input.
- **Returning zero for every failure:** that confuses invalid input with a real zero.
- **Ignoring range:** a syntactically numeric value can still exceed int bounds.
- **Reasoning about stack allocation or guaranteed wrapper allocation:** the language specifies values and references, while the JVM chooses storage and optimization.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **String to int:** `Integer.parseInt(text)`.
- **String to Integer:** `Integer.valueOf(text)`.
- **int to String:** `Integer.toString(value)` or `String.valueOf(value)`.
- **Invalid or out of range:** `NumberFormatException`.
- **Not a cast:** parsing interprets characters; choose trimming, radix, and error handling explicitly.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I parse a String with `Integer.parseInt`, which returns a primitive int. If I need the wrapper, I use `Integer.valueOf`. For example, `Integer.parseInt("2A", 16)` returns 42. Invalid syntax, embedded or surrounding whitespace, and an out-of-range value can produce `NumberFormatException`, so an input boundary should validate, map, or propagate that failure according to its contract.

To convert an int back to text, I use `Integer.toString(value)` or `String.valueOf(value)`. This is not casting: `(int) "42"` does not compile because no Java conversion interprets that reference as numeric text. Primitive numeric casts and compatible reference casts are separate language conversions; parsing and formatting are library operations.

questions.question: What happens when you cast a double 9.99 to an int in Java — does it round or truncate?
questions.title: Truncation vs Rounding in Java double to int Cast
questions.direct_answer: Casting the finite in-range `double` value 9.99 to `int` gives 9: Java removes the fractional part toward zero; it does not round to the nearest integer. Special boundaries matter too: NaN becomes 0, and values beyond the int range clamp to `Integer.MIN_VALUE` or `Integer.MAX_VALUE`. Use `Math.round`, `floor`, `ceil`, or decimal rounding when those are the intended rules.

interviewer_intent.testing: A classic output-prediction gotcha — truncation vs rounding surprises many freshers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting (int) 9.9 to give 10 — it gives 9; truncation always goes toward zero
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Math.round() for nearest-integer rounding, and Math.ceil()/Math.floor() for ceiling/floor

sections.title: The Cast Operator Is a Chopper, Not a Rounder
sections.content:
For the value in the question, `(int) 9.99` evaluates to **9**. A floating-to-integer cast removes the fractional part toward zero, so `(int) -3.7` becomes -3 rather than -4. It does not choose the nearest integer.

Java also defines edge cases. NaN converts to zero. A finite or infinite value above the int range becomes `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, and one below the range becomes `Integer.MIN_VALUE`. This differs from narrowing one integer type to another, which discards high-order bits.

Choose the operation that matches the rule: cast for truncation, `Math.round` for its nearest-integer rule, `Math.floor` toward negative infinity, and `Math.ceil` toward positive infinity. For money, use `BigDecimal` and an explicit `RoundingMode`.

sections.title: What Happens to 9.99 When You Cast It to int
sections.content:
The diagram traces exactly what the JVM does when it executes `(int) 9.99`. There is no intelligence here — just mechanical removal of the decimal part. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["9.99
(double)"] B["Drop the
fractional part
(.99 is gone)"] C["9
(int)"] A -->|"(int) cast"| B B -->|"result"| C D["9.99 is closer to 10
but we still get 9"] C -.->|"not rounded"| D style D fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,color:#92400e ``` And here is the negative-number case that trips people up: ```mermaid flowchart LR X["-3.7
(double)"] Y["Truncate toward zero
(-.7 is gone)"] Z["-3
(int)"] X -->|"(int) cast"| Y Y -->|"result"| Z W["Math.floor(-3.7)
would give -4"] Z -.->|"differs from floor"| W style W fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#3b82f6,color:#1e3a8a ``` For positive numbers, truncation and floor give the same answer. For negative numbers they differ. That is the gotcha.

sections.title: Cast vs Round at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Cast double to int|~Truncates|(int) 9.99 is 9|drops the fraction|fast, single instruction
blue|Toward zero|~Not floor|(int) -3.7 is -3|not -4|differs from Math.floor
emerald|Round properly|~Math.round()|returns a long|cast to int|nearest integer
rose|Ceil and floor|~Math.ceil rounds up|Math.floor rounds down|capacity/pagination|money: use BigDecimal

sections.title: Every Rounding Behavior Side by Side
sections.content:
Seeing all four behaviors in one place makes the differences click — the same two numbers run through a plain cast, `Math.round`, `Math.ceil`, and `Math.floor` so you can compare the outputs directly.

```java
public class DoubleTruncationDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println((int) 9.99);        // 9   — truncates
        System.out.println((int) -3.7);        // -3  — toward zero, not -4

        System.out.println((int) Math.round(9.99)); // 10 — nearest
        System.out.println((int) Math.round(-3.7)); // -4 — nearest

        System.out.println((int) Math.ceil(9.1));   // 10 — round up
        System.out.println((int) Math.floor(9.9));  // 9  — round down
    }
}
```

The pair to stare at is `(int) -3.7` giving `-3` while `Math.floor(-3.7)` gives `-4` — that single divergence between truncation and floor on negatives is the exact trap interviewers set.

sections.title: The Bug: Trusting the Cast to Do Your Rounding
sections.content:
This is the line that quietly produces wrong totals. The variable is even named `rounded`, which is exactly what the developer assumed would happen.

```java
double price = 9.99;
int rounded = (int) price; // 9 — NOT 10; the cast truncates
```

The code compiles, runs, and ships — it just gives the wrong number. There is no error to catch, which is why this kind of bug survives all the way to production reports that are off by a cent or a unit.

sections.title: The Fix: Say "Round" When You Mean Round
sections.content:
If you want nearest-integer behavior, ask for it explicitly. `Math.round` does the comparison the cast refuses to do.

```java
double price = 9.99;
int rounded = (int) Math.round(price); // 10 — nearest integer
```

One detail trips people here: `Math.round` returns a `long`, so you still cast it to `int`. Reach for `Math.ceil` when you must always round up — like pages or boxes — and `Math.floor` when you must always round down.

sections.title: When Truncation Matters
sections.content: Use a direct int cast when discarding the fraction toward zero is exactly the contract, such as extracting the integral part of a bounded measured value. Use `floor` for a mathematical lower bound, `ceil` for an upper bound such as positive page counts after correct division, and `round` for Java's nearest-integer rule. Check range before narrowing when saturation would hide bad data. Use BigDecimal for exact decimal business rules.

sections.title: The Off-by-One Bugs Truncation Loves to Cause
sections.content:
- **Expecting `(int) 9.99` to become 10:** casting is not nearest rounding.
- **Calling truncation round-down:** for negative values it moves toward zero, unlike floor.
- **Assuming every narrowing overflow wraps:** floating-to-integer conversion clamps after truncation; integer-to-integer narrowing follows different rules.
- **Ignoring Math.round's return type:** the double overload returns long, so a further checked narrowing may be needed.
- **Explaining the rule as a CPU-speed choice:** Java defines the result independently of a particular processor instruction.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`(int) 9.99` is 9.**
- **Finite in-range cast:** discards the fraction toward zero.
- **Negative example:** `(int) -3.7` is -3, while `floor(-3.7)` is -4.
- **Edge cases:** NaN becomes 0; out-of-range values clamp to int min/max.
- **Choose explicitly:** cast, round, floor, ceil, or decimal rounding express different rules.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Casting `9.99` to int returns 9 because Java truncates the finite in-range value toward zero; it does not round to the nearest integer. For example, `(int) -3.7` is -3, whereas `Math.floor(-3.7)` is -4.

If nearest-integer behavior is required, I use `Math.round` and then handle its return type and range deliberately. `floor` and `ceil` express directional rules. The cast also has defined edge cases: NaN becomes zero and a value outside int range clamps to the nearest int endpoint. For financial amounts, I avoid binary floating-point rounding guesses and use BigDecimal with the required rounding mode.
